title: The Bird in the Lightning Oak
part: PART ONE: LIGHT WIND FROM THE WEST

pages.text:
*Sky Report: still, warm, a strange hush before something.*

Dawn broke in shades of pale apricot. Pip slipped out of the hedge’s thorny heart and hopped toward the edge, where the ground sloped away into the tall grass. There, standing alone and jagged against the sky, was the Lightning Oak. Its bark was scarred and black, split by a bolt two summers ago. Nobody went there. The older sparrows crossed their feathers and flew the long way around, muttering about bad luck and old ghosts.

Pip did not believe in ghosts. She believed in wind.

She reached the base of the tree and pressed her beak against the rough, cold bark. It smelled of damp earth and ozone, a sharp tang that made the fuzz on her neck stand up. She began to climb. One step. Two. Her tiny claws gripped the ridges. Up she went, past the low branches, past the knot of lichen, higher until her wings trembled with the effort.

At the top, near the split in the trunk, was a hollow dark as a pupil.

She leaned forward and called out, her voice small in the vast morning air. "Hello? Is someone home?"

Silence stretched. Then, from the depths, came a dry cough that cracked like a dry seed shell. A voice drifted out, raspy and rough.

"Go away. I'm not home."
pages.image: A tiny brown sparrow with a crooked left tail feather climbs the rough black bark of a huge, lightning-split oak tree at dawn, looking into a dark hollow near the top.

pages.text:
A shadow shifted in the darkness of the hollow. A head emerged. It was ragged, feathers sticking out in every direction, and one eye was covered by a patch of matted grey feathers. The other eye was bright, sharp, and gleaming like a drop of sap. Half his tail feathers were missing, leaving a jagged edge that trembled slightly in the breeze.

He looked at Pip. He looked at her for a long, long time.

"You're the runt," he said. His voice was still dry, but there was a spark in it now.

"I'm Pip," she corrected, puffing her chest out to look as big as she could.

"Hmph." The old bird shook his head. "You're not the runt. I was the runt. You're a runt-in-training." He hopped back into the hollow, leaving a trail of dust. "I do not train fledglings. I never have. I am retired. I am old. I am done."

Pip did not move. She stood on the topmost branch, her toes curled tight. "I'm not a fledgling," she said, though she knew that was a lie. "I'm just... early."
pages.image: An old, ragged sparrow with one eye covered by a patch of grey fur and a jagged tail looks down from a tree hollow at a tiny, determined sparrow standing on the branch below.

pages.text:
"I want to be a Storm-Sparrow," Pip said, the words sitting heavy in her mouth like a seed she was swallowing whole. She knew the rules. She knew she was too small, too light, and too slow for the Elders' liking. But she was going to do it anyway.

The old bird said nothing. He watched a single leaf drift past the hollow, tumble, catch the air, and disappear over the hedge. The moment stretched out, thin and golden, holding its breath with them.

Then he spoke. "Who said you can't?"

"Everyone," Pip replied, her voice dropping to a whisper. "Uncle Dorn. Elder Marra. Even the seeds, sometimes, when I try to carry them."

Tuck cocked his one good eye. "Have you asked the sky?"

Pip blinked. She tilted her head, the way she always did when she was thinking, her crooked tail feather twitching in the draft. "The sky doesn't answer."

"Doesn't it?" Tuck’s dry voice softened, just a fraction, like a rustle of dry leaves settling down. "You'd be surprised."
pages.image: A tiny sparrow with bright black eyes looks up at an old, one-eyed sparrow in a tree hollow; a single leaf drifts past them in the golden morning light.

pages.text:
"Here is the deal," Tuck said, his head emerging fully now. He looked less like a crumpled leaf and more like a bird, though a very tired one. "One lesson. First light tomorrow. Top of the oak."

Pip’s heart beat fast. A tiny drum in her ribs.

"Just one?"

"If you can stay in the air for one hundred wingbeats without landing," Tuck said, "I will consider a second." He paused. "If you land before then, you go home and stay low. Where you belong."

A grim gleam lit up his good eye. "You will be flying into the morning updraft. It throws big birds around. It likes small ones."

Pip did not think about the danger. She did not think about the height. She thought about the sky. Vast. Waiting.

"Yes."

The word came out fast. Sharp. Bright.

Her crooked tail feather twitched with the motion.
pages.image: A tiny sparrow stands on a high branch, looking up at an old sparrow with a sharp, gleaming eye; the background shows a clear, bright blue sky with soft clouds.

pages.text:
On the way back to the hedge, Pip stopped at a puddle in the grass. The water was still, holding the reflection of the morning sky. She looked down and saw a tiny, brown-streaked bird with a crooked tail feather on the left. She looked small and fragile, exactly like she always had.

She watched her reflection for a long time. The water rippled slightly, and her image wavered, but it did not break.

"Small birds stay low," she said to the puddle. Her voice was quiet, barely a whisper.

She lifted her head, and the sky stretched out above her, endless and blue, promising wind and distance and freedom. She looked at it, and for the first time, she did not feel small. She felt ready.

"Well," she said to the sky, "let's find out."
pages.image: A tiny sparrow with a crooked left tail feather looks down at her own reflection in a small puddle in the grass, then looks up at a vast, clear blue sky.
